sentences.text: Baptornis was a genus of aquatic birds that lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
This animal existed from the Coniacian to the Campanian stages, spanning between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
The creature possessed a markedly elongated neck compared to its relatives.
This unusually long neck allowed the bird to strike fish with its sharp beak.
Unlike modern birds, Baptornis had small sharp teeth covering its jaws.
The animal weighed about 7 kg and measured 1 meter in length.
No complete skeletons of Baptornis have been found, so the skeleton of its relative Hesperornis was used for reconstruction.
Its lower legs were flush against its body with feet stretched sideways, making it unable to stand upright.
Coprolites associated with Baptornis contain remains of the sabre-toothed fish Enchodus.
Baptornis provides the only certain record of food for the Hesperornithes group.
Parascaniornis stensioi, previously thought to be a flamingo or loon, is now considered to belong with Baptornis.
Othniel Charles Marsh discovered the first fossils of Baptornis in the 1870s.
Baptornis was one of the first Mesozoic birds known to science, alongside Archaeopteryx.
The type species of the genus Baptornis is Baptornis advenus.
There are 10 recorded fossil occurrences of Baptornis in the Paleobiology Database.
Baptornis held prey in its beak like mergansers rather than spearing it like darters.
The sharp teeth were useful for holding fish firmly, which made up most of its diet.
Baptornis was excellently adapted for swimming and diving but thought to be clumsy on land.
The flat sternum of Baptornis indicates that the muscles controlling its wings were small and weak.
Baptornis were skilled underwater predators capable of maneuvering well by twisting and turning quickly while chasing prey.
Baptornis had a torpedo-like profile and were aerodynamic, facilitating their movements in water.
Baptornis birds likely found walking on land difficult because their legs were positioned far behind their bodies.
Baptornis was likely constantly threatened by large marine reptiles like mosasaurs living beneath the sea surface.
The family Baptornithidae was established for Baptornis due to its peculiar characteristics among Hesperornithes.
The classification of Neogaeornis is debated; it might be a baptornithid or related to modern Gaviiformes or Procellariiformes.
Fossils of the type species Baptornis advenus were found in Kansas, an area covered by the shallow Western Interior Seaway.
Baptornis is also known from Sweden and possibly occurred throughout the Holarctic region.
Fossils of Baptornis are found in limestone rocks that typically form at shorelines, indicating a coastal habitat.
